title: eBPF Tools: Asking the Kernel What's Really Happening
intro: eBPF lets small, safe programs run inside the kernel and report on events as they happen: every process started, every file opened, every disk request. The bcc collection packages dozens of ready-made tools, and they answer questions that sampling can't, such as 'what keeps starting?' and 'how slow is the disk, really?'. On Ubuntu the tools end in -bpfcc. You're on a host that's slower than it should be, with no single process to blame.

steps.prompt: CPU load is high and top shows nothing using much. Short-lived processes can hide between top's refreshes. Trace every new process as it starts.
steps.fake_output:
PCOMM            PID     PPID    RET ARGS
sh               41204   1204      0 /bin/sh -c /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh
check-disk.sh    41204   1204      0 /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh
df               41205   41204     0 /usr/bin/df -h
awk              41206   41204     0 /usr/bin/awk {print $5}
sh               41207   1204      0 /bin/sh -c /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh
check-disk.sh    41207   1204      0 /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh
steps.explanation: A script, check-disk.sh, is being launched over and over by pid 1204, each time spawning df and awk.
steps.why: Processes that live for a few milliseconds never show in top, yet starting thousands of them a minute costs real CPU. execsnoop catches each one at the moment it starts, with its parent and arguments. Here a monitoring agent is running a check in a tight loop, probably a misconfigured interval.

steps.prompt: An application fails to start with an unhelpful 'configuration error'. See which files it tries to open: trace opens for pid 5120.
steps.fake_output:
PID    COMM       FD ERR PATH
5120   shop-api    3   0 /etc/ld.so.cache
5120   shop-api    3   0 /app/config/default.yaml
5120   shop-api   -1   2 /app/config/production.yaml
5120   shop-api   -1   2 /etc/shop/production.yaml
steps.explanation: It opened default.yaml, then failed to find production.yaml in two places (ERR 2 is 'no such file').
steps.why: This answers 'which file is it actually looking for?' without reading the source or attaching a debugger. ERR 2 is ENOENT and 13 is EACCES (permission denied). strace can do the same and slows the process badly; eBPF tools trace with very little overhead, which is why they can be used on production hosts.

steps.prompt: Storage is suspected. Measure how long disk requests actually take: print a latency histogram covering 10 seconds, once.
steps.explanation: Most requests take under a millisecond, and a second group of about 600 takes 130 to 520 milliseconds.
steps.why: An average would have said 'about 20 ms' and hidden both facts. The histogram shows two populations: a healthy device, and occasional requests that are hundreds of times slower. That second hump is what users feel as random stalls. Two-humped latency usually means two causes: here, fast reads, and writes stuck behind something flushing. iostat's 'await' can't show this.

steps.prompt: Check whether processes are waiting for a turn on the CPU: print a run-queue latency histogram for 10 seconds, once.
steps.explanation: Nearly everything gets a CPU within a few microseconds.
steps.why: Run-queue latency is how long a ready thread waits before it's given a CPU. This is healthy. Tens of milliseconds here would mean CPU saturation, even when average utilisation looks moderate, and inside a container it's also how CPU throttling from a low limit shows up. It's a direct measurement of what 'load average' only hints at.

steps.prompt: The ready-made tools are bpftrace programs underneath, and you can write one-liners. Count 'openat' system calls by process name until you press Ctrl+C.
steps.explanation: df and the check script open files far more than anything else, confirming the runaway check.
steps.why: The program reads: on each openat system call, add one to a map keyed by the process name; print the map at the end. That pattern, a probe, an optional filter, and an aggregation, covers a huge range of questions. Aggregating in the kernel and printing a summary is what keeps the cost low, compared with printing every event.
